owner.name: Corinne Ballard
owner.heading: The person who answers when the scope slips
owner.bio: Corinne Ballard spent her early career on the other side of this contract — running a building for someone else and chasing a cleaning company that never sent the same two people twice. She started Keyholder to be the version she could not hire: a written scope, a crew listed by name, and a sheet in the building that says who was there and what got done. She still walks every new building herself, and her number is the one on the proposal.

faq.q: Do you clean during business hours?
faq.a: Rarely. Most buildings on our route are done after close, between six and midnight, so nobody has to work around a mop bucket. Day-porter coverage during business hours can be added to any contract if your lobby needs it.

faq.q: Who has keys and codes to my building?
faq.a: Named people, and only named people. Everyone assigned to your building is listed on the contract, and that list changes in writing, not quietly. Keys and alarm codes are signed in and out each shift.

faq.q: What happens when something gets missed?
faq.a: Write it on the sign-off sheet or send us a message, and we are back before the next scheduled visit at no charge. The sheet tells us who was in the building and what they covered, so we can usually answer what happened the same day.

faq.q: Do you bring your own equipment and supplies?
faq.a: Yes — machines, chemicals and cloths are ours and stay on our truck. Consumables your building hands to the public, like liners, paper and soap, are itemized at cost, or you can keep buying your own if that is cheaper for you.

faq.q: How long is a contract, and how do I get out of it?
faq.a: Month to month after the first ninety days, with thirty days notice either way. We would rather keep a building because the work holds up than because a term said we get to.

about.heading: Facilities managers do not need another vendor to chase
about.body: The complaint we hear on every walkthrough is the same one: nobody knows who was in the building last night, the scope drifted six months ago, and the invoice never changed. So we run the boring version on purpose. Every task is written down with a frequency beside it. The people assigned to your building are named on the contract. A dated sheet stays on site so you can see what was covered without calling anyone. If the scope needs to change, it changes in writing and the price moves with it.

standards.title: A scope you can hold us to

process.title: Walk the building
process.desc: We meet you on site — after hours if that is easier — and measure the cleanable square footage room by room. Restroom count, floor types and trash volume all get written down.

process.title: Written scope and price
process.desc: You get a task list with a frequency against each line and a price against the whole thing. Nothing is ordered, scheduled or charged until you have read it.

process.title: Crew assigned by name
process.desc: The people who will be in your building are named on the contract, issued their own access, and walked through the scope with you before the first shift.

process.title: Sign-off, every visit
process.desc: A dated sheet stays in the building. Anything missed gets written on it, and we are back before the next scheduled visit to close it out.

niche.pricingNote: Rates are per square foot of cleanable space, billed monthly against a written contract. Consumables are itemized at cost unless your building would rather supply its own. Every figure on this page is a starting structure, not a quote — the walkthrough sets the real number.
niche.estimatorNote: A starting figure only. Square footage is the biggest single driver of a janitorial price, but restroom count, floor type and how much trash a building makes all move it. Nothing here is a quote.
